claims.text: The target alloy is a refractory Nb–Ta–W–Mo–V high-entropy alloy.
A Nb–Ta–W–Mo–V refractory HEA typically has a dendritic microstructure.
Pack cementation at 900°C for 10 hours using an aluminum-containing powder mixture will diffuse aluminum into the HEA surface.
The aluminization treatment will form an aluminide-rich precursor layer on the Nb–Ta–W–Mo–V HEA.
Sufficient aluminum activity is required to support formation of an Al2O3 scale.
During exposure in air at 1200°C, the aluminide precursor will transform into a continuous Al2O3 scale.
Formation of a protective alumina scale is thermodynamically favored at 1200°C.
Alumina is stable and has low ionic and oxygen transport at high temperature.
Alumina provides an effective barrier to oxygen penetration and grows slowly at temperatures up to about 1300°C.
The alumina scale formed on the aluminized HEA will be well-adherent.
Low oxygen transport through the alumina scale will reduce oxygen ingress and oxidation of the underlying alloy.
After 50 hours in air at 1200°C, the aluminized HEA will have a statistically significantly lower oxidation rate and weight gain than the untreated alloy.
After exposure, the aluminized HEA will have a thinner and more adherent oxide scale than the untreated alloy.
An untreated Nb–Ta–W–Mo–V HEA exposed to air at 1200°C for 50 hours typically forms a thick, poorly adherent scale and exhibits high weight gain.
The proposed benefit should extend to refractory HEAs with compositions similar to Nb–Ta–W–Mo–V when pack-cementation conditions are controlled.
Excessive aluminum uptake may create brittle intermetallic phases that negate the oxidation-resistance benefit.
Weight gain per unit area, scale thickness, scale continuity, and phase composition can be compared between aluminized and untreated samples after identical oxidation exposure.
Failure of the treated samples to show a statistically significant weight-gain reduction together with a thinner, continuous alumina scale would falsify the hypothesis.
